newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Austrian conservatives up stakes in CA sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Austrian conservatives up stakes in CA sale.

text.p: Austrian conservatives deepened a rift in the coalition on Wednesday when they proposed to outlaw the future sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria in an attempt to force the finance minister's hand.

The bill, drawn up by the People's Party, seeks to block "socialist" Bank Austria's proposed takeover of conservative stronghold Creditanstalt by excluding public bodies from the privatisation process. The conservatives rule in coalition with Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats.
The City of Vienna, also dominated by the Social Democrats, effectively controls Bank Austria through holding company AV-Z and guarantees its liabilities.
Defending his bill, People's Party whip Andreas Khol accused the Social Democrats of acting against the spirit of the two partys' coalition agreement.
"I hope the Social Democrats recognise the seriousness of the situation...I will do everything in my power to prevent the creation of a banking behemoth," he said.
Social Democrat whip Peter Kostelka sounded a warning: "This adds even more fuel to an already volatile situation."

Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima was unbowed by conservative criticism and reminded the People's Party that failure to sell the state's 70 percent of Creditanstalt ordinary shares to the top bidder would draw EU scrutiny.
"The People's Party will (also) have to represent its position to the Austrian public if it causes the government to lose out on billions of schillings," Klima said.
Bank Austria has outbid its rivals for Creditanstalt by at least one billion schillings, putting up some 16 billion ($1.47 billion) for the state's stake which is worth 14.5 billion at market prices.
Klima has promised to name a buyer by year-end. He must choose between Bank Austria, a consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali and 79-year-old entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek.

Khol's bill, an amendment to an existing bank privatisation law, needs the backing of a third of MPs to force a parliamentary vote, probably early next month. The new law would be retroactive to December 1.
The People's Party needs the support of the far-right Freedom Party to push through the bill with a simple majority.

Last week the two voted together to urge the government to carry out a far-reaching privatisation of the nation's overcrowded banking sector but Freedom Party chief Joerg Haider was more cautious in his response to the latest motion.
"The content is not suited to preventing a sale to Bank Austria because the AV-Z is neither a regional public body nor a fund. It is an administrative body," Haider said.
Behind the scenes, meanwhile, Creditanstalt's board tried desperately to pull the strings in Europe's longest running privatisation and preempt a takeover by Bank Austria.

Having opposed successive bids, including the EA-Generali group's most recent offer, Creditanstalt's board appears to have done an about-face since its arch-rival Bank Austria entered the fray last week.
"It would be a real catastrophe if what is left in Austria is one big savings bank controlled by the City of Vienna," a source close to the bank's management told Reuters.
The EA-Generali consortium, which also includes savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank AG (First Austrian), presented an excellent solution, he added.
"Creditanstalt and First Austrian would complement each other well," the source said.
($1=10.88 Schilling)
